newsitem.title: USA: U.S MUNICIPAL FOCUS - prices slip, home sales rise.
newsitem.headline: U.S MUNICIPAL FOCUS - prices slip, home sales rise.

text.p: U.S. municipal bond prices edged down about one-quarter of a point as the market, much like U.S. Treasury bonds, reacted to a surprising surge in August new home sales.

Sales of new single-family homes jumped 4.7 percent in August to a seasonally adjusted, annual pace of 832,000 units, the highest level since April 1986. Economists polled by Reuters had expected an annual pace of 744,000 units.
"The selling is not that intense, but people are just backing off bids," a trader said, explaining that today's activity was fairly light, as can be typical on a Monday.
The market's bearish tone also was set by some key findings in the Chicago Purchasing Managers Index for September, which showed the prices paid index leaped to 59.3 from 51.8 August.
Traders said players might be reluctant to take sizable positions ahead of the U.S. payrolls data, due on Friday, which for the past few months have triggered sharp volatility.
The data are expected to show a 166,000 increase in jobs, according to a Reuters consensus survey of economists, while the unemployment rate is anticipated rising 0.1 percentage point to 5.2 percent.
The market last week was largely relieved when the policy-making body of the Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged.

While traders said the bank still might be persuaded to hike rates before the Nov 5 elections, they noted that such a move likely would require overwhelmingly strong evidence of economic strength. "That's a distant bet," one added.

The long-end of the market was looking ahead to the sale this week of approximately $270 million of Denver City and County Airport bonds, while short-term traders awaited the sale of $1.6 billion of New York City notes on October 1.

While bidwanted lists were fairly light, actively quoted issues included Cook County Illinois Capital Improvement bonds of November 2022, which carry a 5-7/8 percent coupon. They were bid at 99-1/4, down 1/4 of a point from levels seen on Friday.
Denver Colorado City and County Airport Revenue Series A of November 2025, which have a 5-1/2 percent coupon, were bid at 5.83 percent, up three basis points.

The December municipal bond futures traded on the Chicago Board of Trade edged down eight ticks to 113-29/32, while the December U.S. Treasury bond futures fell the same amount to 109-7/32. This left the MOB spread at 150 ticks.
Traders speculated that the MOB, which has fallen around 20 ticks from a few weeks ago, is unlikely to tumble much further, as new issues remain in fairly short supply.
The Standard & Poor's Corp Blue list, a gauge of the secondary market's size, stood at $1.1 billion, a level that is considered only moderate.
